# The Bridge Over Nothing

The river left our town in the spring of 1987, and the bridge stayed behind.

It happened the way these things happen, which is to say slowly and then all at once. Three weeks of rain. A levee upstream that nobody had inspected since Eisenhower. One morning the Calloway River was where it had always been, brown and patient under the iron trusses of the Main Street Bridge, and the next morning it was a mile and a quarter east, cutting a new path through the Hendricks soybean fields as if it had been planning the move for years and was only waiting for an excuse.

The engineers came out from the capital. They walked the old channel in rubber boots and pointed at things. They said the river would not be coming back, that the new course was lower and the water would prefer it now, the way water always prefers the easiest way down. They said the bridge was structurally sound but functionally obsolete, which my grandmother said was the most honest description of a retired person she had ever heard.

There was talk of tearing it down. There was talk of selling the iron for scrap. A man from a city I had never heard of offered to buy the whole thing and reassemble it over a creek on his property, and for a while it seemed like that might happen. Then the town council met in the Methodist fellowship hall and voted, eleven to two, to keep it.

Nobody could quite say why. The minutes from that meeting, which I have read, contain only the vote and a note that the coffee urn was malfunctioning.

---

So the bridge stayed. It still stands over the old riverbed, which filled in over the years with grass, then wildflowers, then a scattering of cottonwoods whose seeds must have been waiting in the mud all along. In June the meadow beneath the bridge goes white with Queen Anne's lace. Deer bed down in the long grass where the catfish used to lie. Children who were born after 1987 have never known it as anything but a bridge over a field, and they find nothing strange in it, the way children find nothing strange in anything that was already there when they arrived.

Every four years the town paints it. The same green, a dark bottle green that the hardware store has to special-order. It costs more than you would think. There is a line in the municipal budget, between road salt and the library's large-print collection, that says *Bridge Maintenance*, and every year someone at the budget meeting asks what it's for, and every year someone else explains, and the line stays.

---

My grandmother crossed the bridge every day until she died.

She lived on the east side of Main, and the post office was on the west side, and she could have walked around. The street runs right up to the abutments now; you can step off the curb and cross the meadow in the same number of steps. But she took the bridge. Up the gentle incline of the deck, past the plaque from 1911, over the middle span where the river had been deepest, and down the other side. Every day. Rain or snow.

When I was twelve I asked her why. I had just learned the phrase "a waste of time" and was eager to apply it to everything.

She stopped in the middle of the bridge and leaned on the rail. Below us a meadowlark was sitting on a fence post someone had planted in the old channel.

"Your grandfather proposed to me right here," she said. "In 1954. The water was high that year. I could hardly hear him."

I said something about how the water wasn't there anymore.

"No," she agreed. "And he isn't either." She looked down at the grass for a while. "But I'm not going to start walking around things just because they're gone."

I didn't understand what she meant. I thought I did, for years, and then later I understood that I hadn't, and I suspect there are still layers to it I haven't reached.

---

Here is what I think now, at forty-one, having moved away and come back, having lost some things of my own.

We are told to move on. We are told that the healthy thing is to adapt, to take the new path, to prefer the easiest way down like water does. And there is wisdom in that. The river was right to move. It didn't owe us anything.

But people are not rivers. We are the things rivers leave behind. We are bridges, built at great expense for a particular crossing, and when the crossing is gone we remain, shaped exactly to the absence. You can tear down a bridge like that, and some people do, and I don't blame them. Or you can keep it painted. You can keep walking over it. You can let the meadow grow underneath and learn the names of the flowers that come up where the water used to be.

I don't think my grandmother was clinging to the past. I think she was keeping faith with it, which is different. Clinging is when you refuse to let the meadow grow. Faith is when you walk over the meadow every morning, and notice the Queen Anne's lace, and remember the sound of the water, and hold both at once.

---

I walked the bridge this morning. They painted it last fall, so the green is still bright, and the rivets catch the early light. At the middle span I stopped where she used to stop and leaned on the rail.

A girl of maybe seven was down in the meadow with her father, picking something—clover, I think. She looked up and saw me and waved, the uncomplicated wave of a child who has never once wondered why a bridge would cross a field.

I waved back.

Then I went on across, down the other side, and went about my day, the way you do. Carrying the river with me. Not walking around it.

I want to avoid overused tropes like lighthouse keepers or AI musing on consciousness, so I'm brainstorming something fresher—maybe a piano tuner working in a house after a death, or a town where the river shifted course and the bridge now spans dry land, yet people still cross it out of habit.

I'll write it as a short story from the perspective of someone who grew up there—the river moved in 1987 after a flood, the bridge remains over a meadow, and the town keeps repainting it anyway. The grandmother crosses it every day, and the piece is really about fidelity to what's gone, love expressed as habit, ending with the narrator crossing and noticing something new.
